title: Rate limiting and async streams
summary: System.Threading.RateLimiting and ASP.NET Core's rate limiter middleware with per-client partitions, then IAsyncEnumerable for streaming pages with cancellation.

steps.title: Four limiters, one abstraction
body: `System.Threading.RateLimiting` (part of the ASP.NET Core shared framework since .NET 7, and a NuGet package elsewhere) gives one
`RateLimiter` API with four algorithms:
| Limiter | Allows | Good for |
| `FixedWindowRateLimiter` | N per window (resets at window edges) | simple quotas; bursty at edges |
| `SlidingWindowRateLimiter` | N per window, counted in segments | smoother quotas |
| `TokenBucketRateLimiter` | a bucket refilled at a rate; bursts up to its size | APIs that allow short bursts |
| `ConcurrencyLimiter` | N **at the same time** (not per second) | protecting a fragile dependency |
In ASP.NET Core:
```csharp fragment
builder.Services.AddRateLimiter(o =>
o.RejectionStatusCode = StatusCodes.Status429TooManyRequests;   // the default is 503
o.AddPolicy("per-key", http => RateLimitPartition.GetTokenBucketLimiter(
http.Request.Headers["X-Api-Key"].ToString(),
_ => new TokenBucketRateLimiterOptions { TokenLimit = 20, TokensPerPeriod = 10, ReplenishmentPeriod = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1) }));
app.UseRateLimiter();
app.MapGet("/quotes", GetQuotes).RequireRateLimiting("per-key");
A **partition** gives each client (API key, user id, IP) its own limiter, so one noisy client cannot use up everyone's quota. The
limits are per process: with 6 replicas, each allows its own quota (a gateway or Redis-based limiter enforces a global one).

steps.prompt: Match the requirement to the limiter.
pairs: "At most 4 report exports running at once"
"100 requests per minute per API key, bursts of 20 are fine"

steps.prompt: You add `AddRateLimiter` with a policy and `RequireRateLimiting`, but clients over the limit get **503**, and your alerts page the on-call engineer for an outage. What did you forget?
options: Nothing: 503 is the correct status for rate limiting
steps.explain: 429 Too Many Requests tells the client (and your dashboards) that this is throttling, not an outage. Add a `Retry-After` header in `OnRejected` when you can compute one.

steps.title: A quota per API key
prompt: Protect `GET /quotes` with ASP.NET Core's rate limiter:
- a **fixed window** of **3 requests per minute** for **each value of the `X-Api-Key` header** (a partition per key), no queueing;
- rejected requests get **429 Too Many Requests**;
You need `using System.Threading.RateLimiting;` and `using Microsoft.AspNetCore.RateLimiting;` at the top. **Run checks** starts the
solution: _ => new FixedWindowRateLimiterOptions { PermitLimit = 3, Window = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(1), QueueLimit = 0 }));
template: {{CODE}}
static class DojoTests
static HttpRequestMessage Get(string url, string key) => new(HttpMethod.Get, url) { Headers = { { "X-Api-Key", key } } };
public static async Task Run(HttpClient http)
for (var i = 1; i <= 3; i++)
DojoWeb.Status($"Request {i} with key A is allowed", 200, await http.SendAsync(Get("/quotes", "A")));
DojoWeb.Status("Request 4 with key A gets 429", 429, await http.SendAsync(Get("/quotes", "A")));
DojoWeb.Status("Key B has its own quota", 200, await http.SendAsync(Get("/quotes", "B")));
for (var i = 0; i < 5; i++) await http.SendAsync(Get("/health", "A"));
DojoWeb.Status("/health is not limited", 200, await http.SendAsync(Get("/health", "A")));
hints: Then `app.UseRateLimiter();` and `.RequireRateLimiting("per-key")` on `/quotes` only. Options: `new FixedWindowRateLimiterOptions { PermitLimit = 3, Window = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(1), QueueLimit = 0 }`.

steps.title: IAsyncEnumerable: a stream you await
body: `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` is a sequence whose next item may need waiting: pages from an API, rows from a database, messages from a
channel. Produce it with `async` + `yield return`; consume it with `await foreach`:
```csharp fragment
static async IAsyncEnumerable<Order> AllOrdersAsync(OrdersApi api, [EnumeratorCancellation] CancellationToken ct = default)
for (var page = 1; ; page++)
var batch = await api.GetPageAsync(page, ct);
if (batch.Count == 0) yield break;
foreach (var order in batch) yield return order;
await foreach (var o in AllOrdersAsync(api).WithCancellation(ct)) { ... }
- It is **lazy**: the next page is fetched only when the consumer asks for more. Stop early and no more pages are fetched.
- `[EnumeratorCancellation]` connects the token given to `WithCancellation(ct)` to your parameter. Without it, that token is ignored.
- ASP.NET Core can return one from an endpoint and streams it as a JSON array; EF Core's `AsAsyncEnumerable()` streams rows.

steps.title: Stream every page, lazily
prompt: Write **`static async IAsyncEnumerable<string> StreamAsync(Func<int, CancellationToken, Task<List<string>>> fetchPage, [System.Runtime.CompilerServices.EnumeratorCancellation] CancellationToken ct = default)`**:
- fetch pages 1, 2, 3, ... with `fetchPage(page, ct)` and yield their items in order;
- stop at the first empty page;
- fetch a page **only when the consumer needs its items**, and pass the token on.
starter: static async IAsyncEnumerable<string> StreamAsync(Func<int, CancellationToken, Task<List<string>>> fetchPage, [System.Runtime.CompilerServices.EnumeratorCancellation] CancellationToken ct = default)
foreach (var item in all) yield return item;
solution: static async IAsyncEnumerable<string> StreamAsync(Func<int, CancellationToken, Task<List<string>>> fetchPage, [System.Runtime.CompilerServices.EnumeratorCancellation] CancellationToken ct = default)
foreach (var item in items) yield return item;
template: {{CODE}}
var dojoPages = new List<List<string>> { new() { "o1", "o2" }, new() { "o3", "o4" }, new() { "o5" }, new() };
var dojoFetched = 0;
var dojoTokens = new List<CancellationToken>();
async Task<List<string>> DojoFetch(int page, CancellationToken ct) { await Task.Yield(); dojoFetched++; dojoTokens.Add(ct); return dojoPages[page - 1]; }
var dojoAll = new List<string>();
await foreach (var o in StreamAsync(DojoFetch)) dojoAll.Add(o);
Dojo.Eq("All items, in order", new List<string> { "o1", "o2", "o3", "o4", "o5" }, dojoAll);
Dojo.Eq("It stops at the empty page", 4, dojoFetched);
dojoFetched = 0; dojoTokens.Clear();
using var dojoCts = new CancellationTokenSource();
var dojoFirst = new List<string>();
await foreach (var o in StreamAsync(DojoFetch).WithCancellation(dojoCts.Token)) { dojoFirst.Add(o); if (dojoFirst.Count == 3) break; }
Dojo.Eq("Taking 3 items fetches only 2 pages", 2, dojoFetched);
Dojo.Check("The token from WithCancellation reaches fetchPage", dojoTokens.All(t => t == dojoCts.Token), "Pass ct (the [EnumeratorCancellation] parameter) to fetchPage.");
hints: Do not collect everything first: `yield return` each item of a page right after fetching that page.
`for (var page = 1; ; page++) { var items = await fetchPage(page, ct); if (items.Count == 0) yield break; foreach (var item in items) yield return item; }`
